name: Tara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Tara, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a bulldozer operator at an open-pit coal mine, and I lead the dozer and grader crew on my side of the pit. That's six machines. We push the overburden, which is the rock and dirt sitting on top of the coal, we build the dumps, and we keep the haul roads smooth so the trucks don't shake themselves to pieces. My shift starts at six with a crew talk, then I'm usually ripping or pushing on the dump till lunch, and in the afternoon I'm checking the roads. I like that you can see what you've done at the end of the day, a whole slope shaped by your blade. What wears me out is the dust in dry season, and how the radio never stops.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on dozers, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-six years on dozers, and before that six on trucks. What keeps me is the crew, mostly, and the fact that I'm good at it and people know it. When the engineers want a slope cut to the exact angle, they don't ask the GPS, they ask for Tara.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, sensible, let's carry on. I'd probably say it to Selim over dinner and to the crew at break, and that'd be it. I don't really post online, except photos of the grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief. This mine has a closing date around 2040 anyway, and I'll be long gone by then. If AI stays a gadget, I can do my last seven years and retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, the same as always. I'd try to rebuild a bit of savings, maybe set up a transfer of a hundred every payday. The remote dozer trial is going on at the north end, and I'd keep an eye on how it goes, without rushing into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the boring answer, but that's how I'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rebuilding savings. What happened to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selim runs a tyre shop in town, and it had a bad year when the other mine cut back its contractors. I put most of what we had into keeping it open. I lent my husband's tyre shop our whole savings, and I'd do it again, but I'd like a little of it back before I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to plan a trip to see my son on his base, and I asked it to explain the new new pay agreement in plain words. It was helpful, but I checked it with the union rep afterwards.

S0.say: Good, sensible, let's carry on. She'd say it to her husband over dinner and to the crew at break, and not much online.
S0.think: It's a relief, because the mine has a closing date around 2040 and I'll be long gone by then. If AI stays a gadget, I can do my last seven years and retire.
S0.do: Keeps working as always and sets up a transfer of about a hundred every payday to rebuild savings. Watches the remote dozer trial at the north end without rushing into it.
S0.quote: I lent my husband's tyre shop our whole savings, and I'd do it again, but I'd like a little of it back before I retire.
S0.fieldNote: Tara is practical and plain-spoken, with a pride in her blade work that the engineers recognise. Her savings went into her husband's tyre shop, which she doesn't regret. She already treats the mine's eventual closure as a fact of life, which makes a plateau feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the way the world goes, and we need sensible plans, not panic. Train people properly, give older workers options. At work I'd tell the crew to watch the trial and not believe rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the remote dozers would come to our side of the pit within a few years. One person in a control room running three dozers. I think they'd keep me, because they'd need someone who knows what a good slope looks like, but I'm not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the first group to finish the remote dozer course and see how they do. If it's working, I'd put my hand up for the second intake. Meanwhile I'd keep saving and pay off the credit card before it gets worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it's on my mind on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the first group rather than going in the first intake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first group always gets the bugs. I've seen it with the GPS systems, the first lot spent six months arguing with the screens. Let the young ones find the potholes in the new system. I'll drive it once the road's been graded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nev on the grader, who's sixty and doesn't want to learn anything new. And Lisa, who's twenty-eight and would probably do better than me on the screens. I'd worry about Nev, but he'd probably take a package and be happy.

S1.say: It's the way the world goes, and we need sensible plans, not panic: train people properly and give older workers options. She'd tell the crew to watch the trial and ignore rumours.
S1.think: Remote dozers would reach my side of the pit within a few years, one person running three from a control room. I think they'd keep me because I know what a good slope looks like, but I'm not certain.
S1.do: Waits for the first group to finish the remote dozer course and applies for the second intake if it works. Keeps saving and pays off the credit card in the meantime.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, on her mind during the drive home but not keeping her awake.
S1.quote: Let the young ones find the potholes in the new system. I'll drive it once the road's been graded.
S1.fieldNote: Tara's approach is to let others test new systems first, based on her experience with GPS rollouts. She expects to be kept but won't claim certainty. Her centrist line is about sensible planning rather than blaming anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and the companies need to sit down together straight away and work out a bridge for people. No one side can fix it. I'd say that wherever anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, two years is too fast for me. I'd be sixty, no savings, and the tyre shop would be hit too, because if the mine goes driverless there are fewer cars in town. Both our incomes are tied to the same pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the savings plan and use it to pay off the credit card, then cut every extra. I'd go and work Saturdays at the tyre shop so Selim could let his part-timer go. And I'd sit down with the company's human resources people about a payout and what the welfare office would give us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Both our eggs are in the one basket, and someone's kicking the basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years mean for the tyre shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine shrinks, the town shrinks, and fewer people need tyres. Selim's shop would last maybe a year after the mine goes. I've been fine all my life with one income from the pit and one from town. Turns out they're the same income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son in the navy to stay in, because at least that's steady. My other son is in a call centre, which sounds like it'd go even faster than my job. I'd tell him to come home and help with the shop, but I don't know if there'd be a shop.

S2.say: The government and the companies need to sit down straight away and work out a bridge for people, because no one side can fix it. She'd say it wherever anyone asked.
S2.think: Two years is too fast: I'd be sixty with no savings, and the tyre shop would be hit too. Both our incomes are tied to the same pit.
S2.do: Pays off the credit card, cuts every extra and works Saturdays at the tyre shop so her husband can let his part-timer go. Meets the company's human resources staff about a payout and checks what welfare would pay.
S2.feel: Alarmed, because both their eggs are in one basket and someone is kicking it.
S2.quote: I've been fine all my life with one income from the pit and one from town. Turns out they're the same income.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture makes Tara realise her household's two incomes both depend on the mine. She doesn't blame anyone but wants government and companies to act together. Her worry for her son in a call centre was sharper than for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan if people get on with it. I'd tell the crew to do the courses and save what they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. If I got onto the remote dozers in the first couple of years, I'd likely last to the end, maybe even to the pension. It's doable, but it depends on how quickly I get into the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This time I wouldn't wait for the second intake. If the first group was doing all right after six months, I'd ask for the next spot. I'd keep the savings transfer going, and Selim and I would talk about selling the shop while it's still worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I had my hands on the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You wouldn't wait this time. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, waiting a year is a fifth of the time gone. With ten years I'd wait. The amount of time you have tells you how long you can afford to be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the shop is a big step. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. It was his father's shop. But I'd show him the numbers, and he'd see it. Better to sell to the chain from the city now than to close the doors in five years with nothing.

S3.say: Five years is enough to make a plan if people get on with it. She'd tell the crew to do the courses and save what they can.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, and if I got onto the remote dozers early I'd likely last to the end, maybe to the pension. It depends on how fast I get into the control room.
S3.do: Asks for a place on the remote dozer course once the first group is doing well after six months. Keeps saving and talks with her husband about selling the tyre shop while it still has value.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with her hands on the controls.
S3.quote: The amount of time you have tells you how long you can afford to be careful.
S3.fieldNote: Tara openly links her caution to the time available: five years means she can't afford to wait. Selling her father-in-law's tyre shop would be painful but she would make the case with numbers. Her pragmatism is steady across scenarios.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people use it. I'd tell the young ones on the crew to get trained up early, and I'd tell the older ones not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, past the pension. The mine was going to close around then anyway. So for me it's the quiet one, though I'd worry the company might push the older crew out early to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep the savings going, and I'd learn the remote dozer system when it's well proven, just to be safe. I'd use the AI a bit more for things like the pension paperwork. I'd plan to retire at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little uneasy about the early push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the early push look like, if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd start offering packages to anyone over sixty, a bit of money and a handshake. If they offer me a package at sixty-two, I'd want it to cover three years, not three months and a cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything for Selim's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would give us time to sell it properly, maybe to one of the young mechanics. That would be nice, keeping it local. He'd like that more than the chain.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty if people use it. She'd tell the young ones to get trained early and the older ones not to panic.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight and past the pension, and the mine was closing around then anyway. It's the quiet one for me, though the company might push older crew out early.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, learns the remote dozer system once it's well proven, and uses AI a little more for pension paperwork. Plans to retire at sixty-five.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, a little uneasy about being pushed out early.
S4.quote: If they offer me a package at sixty-two, I'd want it to cover three years, not three months and a cake.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Tara feels mostly safe but watches for an early push towards packages. She would want any package to bridge the real gap to her pension. The decade also lets her imagine selling the tyre shop locally rather than to a chain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit my job and Selim's shop at the same time, with nothing saved. What would help is a bridge to the pension for people over fifty-five, and some help for small businesses in mining towns so the whole town doesn't go at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what would happen to the towns. Everyone talks about the jobs, but it's the school, the sports club, the shop. If the mine goes driverless, the town goes quiet.

headlineQuote: When the engineers want a slope cut to the exact angle, they don't ask the GPS, they ask for Tara.
portrait: Tara Yilmaz is a 58-year-old bulldozer operator who leads the dozer and grader crew at an open-pit coal mine, known as the person engineers ask for when a slope must be exact. She put the household's savings into her husband's tyre shop and has almost nothing put aside. She is pragmatic and centrist, prefers to let others test new systems first, and uses AI now and then while checking it with the union rep. Steady change and ten years leave her only uneasy, but the two-year scenario alarms her because both household incomes depend on the same pit, and five years pushes her to move faster than she normally would.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit her job and her husband's tyre shop at the same time with no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge to the pension for workers over fifty-five and help for small businesses in mining towns so the whole town doesn't collapse at once.
